# High-fructose corn syrup

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="high-fructose-corn-syrup-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="high-fructose-corn-syrup-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="high-fructose-corn-syrup-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

High-fructose corn syrup in the HMI library has 20 reported results for total mercury from 2 sources.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals measured:</strong>

Total mercury, in 20 results from 1 source.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Form, basis and where the high-fructose corn syrup was sampled; reporting limits decide how many results are non-detects.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask for lot results with a quantification limit well below the limit that applies in the destination market.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
</ul>
</section>


<a id="decision-summary"></a>
## High-fructose corn syrup overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

High-fructose corn syrup in the HMI library has 20 reported results for total mercury from 2 sources.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the high-fructose corn syrup came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.



<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers high-fructose corn syrup, as sold (20 results).<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Results stay on the basis each source reports: as sold or fresh weight, dry weight, or unstated. Dry-weight, as-sold and unstated results are never pooled, and no moisture conversion is applied.

<a id="heavy-metal-contamination-profile"></a>
## Heavy metal contamination profile of high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-007"></a>
<a id="which-metals-and-chemical-species-have-been-investigated-in-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-008"></a>
<a id="what-concentrations-detection-frequencies-and-variability-were-observed-in-each-defined-sampling-frame"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-009"></a>
<a id="which-analyte-questions-are-unassessed-access-blocked-conflicting-or-searched-without-eligible-evidence"></a>

The table holds every extracted high-fructose corn syrup result: one row for each statistic a source reports for a form, group and metal, 20 rows in all, grouped by metal and form; percentiles, ranges and maxima for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Monitoring medians are HMI calculations from individual submissions; non-detects remain intervals between zero and the reporting limit and are never read as zero.

9 rows can be rated against an HMI reference for the same form and basis, 0 rows have a direct same-study comparison, and the rest stay unrated with the reason recorded.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-high-fructose-corn-syrup" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-high-fructose-corn-syrup-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of high-fructose corn syrup, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

High-fructose corn syrup, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤5</td><td>≤5</td><td>185</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤5</td><td>≤5</td><td>185</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>20 reference units; 1 sampling family. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Dufault et al. 2009</td><td>20</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for high-fructose corn syrup, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1-Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>Dufault et al. 2009 is the only compatible sampling family for high-fructose corn syrup, as sold on this basis in the completed high-fructose corn syrup ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali" class="internal" data-slug="sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali" data-no-cite-meta>Dufault et al. 2009</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. It describes the evidence currently in this scope; it is not a worldwide or current-lot benchmark. Source, year and region filters do not change it. Different HMI scopes are not one common ranking.</p></details></div></details><div hidden data-form-reasons><p data-reason="bounds_span_categories" data-title="Non-detect spans the bands">The result is below a reporting limit, and the range from zero to that limit crosses more than one band.</p></div><script type="application/octet-stream" data-explorer-payload data-encoding="base64"></script><div hidden data-explorer-details data-chunk-rows="100"><div hidden data-explorer-chunk="0"><script type="application/octet-stream" data-encoding="base64"></script><div data-evidence-content><p class="hmi-dataset-title"><a href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali" class="internal" data-slug="sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Dufault et al. 2009</a></p><p>High-fructose corn syrup, as sold · Total mercury (tHg) · 1 samples.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Selected finding and reference</p><div class="hmi-selected-result" data-selected-finding><strong class="hmi-finding">&lt;5 µg/kg</strong><span class="hmi-row-note">not detected.</span><p>1 samples. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Mercury enters HFCS through the chlor-alkali manufacturing pathway. Several chemicals are required to make HFCS, including caustic soda and hydrochloric acid, which are used throughout the corn wet-milling process to adjust pH.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, Schnoll R, Lukiw WJ, LeBlanc B, Cornett C, Patrick L, Wallinga D, Gilbert SG, Crider R · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Mercury exposure, nutritional deficiencies and metabolic disruptions may affect learning in children</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Behavioral and Brain Functions 2009, 5:44</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Some HFCS manufacturers have used caustic soda produced at mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants, which carry residual mercury as a byproduct of the electrolytic process; when that mercury-grade caustic soda contacts the product stream, mercury can carry through to the finished syrup.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, Schnoll R, Lukiw WJ, LeBlanc B, Cornett C, Patrick L, Wallinga D, Gilbert SG, Crider R · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Mercury exposure, nutritional deficiencies and metabolic disruptions may affect learning in children</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Behavioral and Brain Functions 2009, 5:44</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Manufacturers using the membrane chlor-alkali process, which does not involve mercury, would not introduce this residual. The pilot study data are consistent with this interpretation: nine of ten samples from Manufacturer A, whose product was largely below the detection limit, suggest membrane-process sourcing, while Manufacturers B and C showed consistently detectable mercury in their HFCS. [[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali]] No study in the library measured pathways for lead, cadmium, arsenic or other metals into high-fructose corn syrup.



<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which forms and regions measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

The HMI reference for total mercury in high-fructose corn syrup, as sold pools 20 subgroup units from 1 sampling family, with a median of below 5 µg/kg and a middle half spanning below 5 (lower quartile) and 185 µg/kg (upper quartile).<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

In one study, total mercury across 9 groups of high-fructose corn syrup ranged from 12 µg/kg (US HFCS manufacturer A, HFCS 42%, sample 3) to 570 µg/kg (US HFCS manufacturer C, HFCS 55%, sample 3); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>



<a id="processing-effects-and-derivatives"></a>
## Processing, cooking and preparation

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

No study in the library measured the same high-fructose corn syrup before and after washing, peeling, drying or cooking for metals, so no processing effect can be stated. Heat does not destroy metals; cooking or drying changes a concentration by moving water or metal, not by removing the element.



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation for high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Controls with evidence for high-fructose corn syrup act at the stages below. Grow corn away from cement plants and other industrial emitters (evidence from corn): maize from the three farms downwind of the plant averaged 230-380 µg/kg lead, against 20 µg/kg at a control farm 18 km upwind; a farm 2.7 km upwind averaged 10 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Abatemi-Usman S, Akindele O, Ayanlade A, Perez M, Attahiru I, Norton G, Feldmann J, Krupp E · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Trace elements concentrations in soil contaminate corn in the vicinity of a cement-manufacturing plant: potential health implications</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Exposure Science &amp; Environmental Epidemiology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/abatemi-usman2023-corn-cement-nigeria">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Blend maize and other grains with rice in infant foods (evidence from corn): infant porridges and cakes mixing rice with maize and other gluten-free grains had median inorganic arsenic of 10 and 8 µg/kg, against 66 and 60 µg/kg for pure rice products; maize’s own share was not measured.<sup class="cite">[[sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Carey M, Donaldson E, Signes-Pastor AJ, Meharg AA · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic">Dilution of rice with other gluten free grains to lower inorganic arsenic in foods for young children in response to European Union regulations provides impetus to setting stricter standards</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLoS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/carey2018-rice-dilution-infant-food-eu-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Irrigate corn with fresh or ground water, not wastewater (evidence from corn): maize irrigated with sewage or industrial wastewater carried 260-550 µg/kg lead and 38-112 µg/kg cadmium; maize irrigated with Nile or ground water in the same governorates carried 30 µg/kg lead and 10 µg/kg cadmium or less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adel S. El-Hassanin, Magdy R. Samak, Gomaa N. Abdel-Rahman, Yahia H. Abu-Sree, Essam M. Saleh · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Risk assessment of human exposure to lead and cadmium in maize grains cultivated in soils irrigated either with low-quality water or freshwater</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxicology Reports 7:10-15</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/el-hassanin2020-egypt-maize-pb-cd">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Keep corn fields away from coal-fired power plants (evidence from corn): maize mercury fell from about 21 µg/kg at 1 km to 4.7-6.7 µg/kg at 3 km and 1.06 µg/kg at 5 km; maize bought at a grocery store more than 55 km away held 0.72 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Ask for origin and lot lead results on maize grain (evidence from corn): western Pacific submissions from 2001-2010 had 24 of 327 lead results above 200 µg/kg against 8 of 890 in Europe, and European exceedances fell to none of 400 in 2014-2020.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Test each lot against the limit for its form (evidence from corn): the EU limits lead at 200 µg/kg and cadmium at 100 µg/kg for cereals, and lead at 100 µg/kg and cadmium at 20 µg/kg for sweet corn, on a wet-weight basis; nickel limits apply from July 2025 for sweet corn (400 µg/kg) and July 2026 for cereals (800 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>

<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for total mercury were 5 µg/kg where sources stated them.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

A useful lot result names the form, the basis and a quantification limit well below the limit that applies.



<a id="procurement-and-process-control"></a>
## Buying and verifying high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-028"></a>
<a id="what-origin-traceability-processing-and-analytical-information-should-a-buyer-request"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-029"></a>
<a id="which-control-or-specification-choices-are-supported-and-which-are-policy-choices-requiring-separate-justification"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-030"></a>
<a id="what-supplier-process-or-test-result-changes-should-trigger-investigation-or-requalification"></a>

No maximum level for metals in high-fructose corn syrup was verified from primary text for this page; buyers should confirm the limit that applies in the destination market.



<a id="finished-product-and-exposure-implications"></a>
## Exposure from high-fructose corn syrup

<a id="hmi-ing-031"></a>
<a id="how-do-inclusion-rate-processing-yield-preparation-and-other-ingredients-affect-a-finished-product-estimate"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-032"></a>
<a id="how-do-consumption-patterns-and-intended-populations-affect-dietary-exposure-interpretation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-033"></a>
<a id="what-conclusions-require-finished-product-measurements-or-a-separate-exposure-assessment"></a>

One review estimated daily mercury intakes from HFCS at up to 28 micrograms per person, calculated from the FDA-collected samples reported in the pilot study and US per capita HFCS consumption data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, Schnoll R, Lukiw WJ, LeBlanc B, Cornett C, Patrick L, Wallinga D, Gilbert SG, Crider R · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Mercury exposure, nutritional deficiencies and metabolic disruptions may affect learning in children</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Behavioral and Brain Functions 2009, 5:44</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-mercury-learning-bbf">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> This is a derived calculation, not a direct dietary intake measurement, and no independent intake study for HFCS mercury was identified in the literature. Concentrations describe the food; individual risk depends on intake, body weight, background exposure and metabolic factors not modeled here.

References identify the sources used in these answers. The Sources index preserves additional discovery links; inclusion there does not mean a source has been reviewed for this assessment. <a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## High-fructose corn syrup FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-high-fructose-corn-syrup" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-high-fructose-corn-syrup" data-question="What heavy metals are found in high-fructose corn syrup?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in high-fructose corn syrup?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports total mercury in high-fructose corn syrup, most often total mercury.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-origins-or-products-of-high-fructose-corn-syrup-measured-lowest" data-anchor="which-origins-or-products-of-high-fructose-corn-syrup-measured-lowest" data-question="Which origins or products of high-fructose corn syrup measured lowest?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which origins or products of high-fructose corn syrup measured lowest?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In one study, total mercury across 9 groups of high-fructose corn syrup ranged from 12 µg/kg (US HFCS manufacturer A, HFCS 42%, sample 3) to 570 µg/kg (US HFCS manufacturer C, HFCS 55%, sample 3); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dufault R, LeBlanc B, Schnoll R, Cornett C, Schweitzer L, Wallinga D, Hightower J, Patrick L, Lukiw WJ · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Mercury from chlor-alkali plants: measured concentrations in food product sugar</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health 2009, 8:2</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dufault2009-hfcs-mercury-chlor-alkali">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
